old: This spice's name rode a relay of tongues — Greek to Aramaic to Arabic to Latin — before settling into English.
Its Arabic form, karāwiyā, named the same curled little seed used to flavor rye bread.
Medieval Latin called it carui, close cousin to the Greek káron it borrowed from.
clues: This kitchen spice gets its name from a long relay of borrowing that began in ancient Greek, yet at every stage it seems to have named the same seed.
These small, curved, ridged brown seeds have a warm, faintly licorice-like bite. They resemble cumin but taste sweeter, and they are the specks in a classic deli rye bread.
It flavors Irish seed cake, sauerkraut and Scandinavian aquavit. In Arabic, one stop on its long relay of borrowing, it was called karawiya.
